accuracy.evidence: The objective is the NGSS K-ESS2-1 wording (use and share observations of local weather conditions to describe patterns over time), and its clarification statement names exactly what the lab does: counting sunny, cloudy and rainy days and noticing that it is usually cooler in the morning than in the afternoon. The diary week (rain, sun, rain, cloud, rain) counts to rainy 3, sunny 1, cloudy 1; every 2 pm reading (14, 17, 12, 15, 13 degrees C) is above its 9 am reading (9, 11, 8, 10, 7), typical of a UK spring week. The afternoon-warmest explanation follows the Met Office: the sun keeps heating the ground after midday and the ground warms the air. Season cards (frost, snow, early dark in winter; 25 degrees C, light at bedtime in summer) are stated for places with four seasons such as the UK, and the adult text says equatorial places may have wet and dry seasons instead.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the real slips for this age: naming the week from the one vivid day (prediction 'Sunny' for sports day in a rainy week, m2, the 'count' tag); thinking the early morning is warmest (prediction 'In the morning', p3, 'morn' tag); calling a single event a pattern (step 4 cards, prediction 'Yes' for one sunny Tuesday, m6, 'one' tag); thinking a pattern must hold every single time (m9, 'always' tag); and expecting the same weather in every season (step 5, m5, 'season' tag).

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab is a weather diary: five window views to record, a Sunny / Cloudy / Rainy block chart filled day by day, paired 9 am and 2 pm thermometers on a 0-20 degrees C scale ending in a morning-versus-afternoon bar chart, a pattern-or-one-day sort and a winter-or-summer sort. No other flagship records observations over days or compares times of day. The shingle gate measures it under 30% against every lab, including the weather instrument and weather type lessons, which have no diary or thermometer comparison.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner does what a scientist does for K-ESS2-1: observes, records, then counts. The chart shows Rainy 3 against Sunny 1, so the sunny day they remembered is shown not to be the pattern; tapping the taller red line five times builds the pattern 'afternoon warmer' and the bar chart then shows it at a glance; sorting sentences makes them say why one day is not a pattern. Step text confirms each idea after the learner has seen it.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: 'Sunny' for the week with a memorable sunny sports day (the chart counts 3 rainy days), 'In the morning' for the warmer time (all five afternoons are warmer), and 'Yes' for whether one sunny Tuesday is a pattern (the sort puts single days in 'Just one day'). The done message names the learner's own prediction.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions with the answer in a rotating position; every wrong option carries its own message: 'count' (count every day; the one you remember best may not be the most common), 'morn' (mornings are usually cooler; the sun warms the air all day), 'one' (that is just one day; a pattern happens again and again), 'season' (frost and snow come in winter), 'always' (a pattern is what usually happens) and 'why' (writing it down cannot change the weather). Wrong moves in the lab are answered the same way, e.g. 'At 9 am it was 9 degrees C. The red line is shorter, so the morning was colder.'

readability.evidence: validate_lessons.py passes both readability limits (the adult text was rewritten into shorter sentences after a first FK 11.9 failure). Kid paragraphs use short sentences and everyday words (window, diary, count, red line, warm), with one idea each. Canvas prompts are one line, day labels and buttons 14-18 px, and each symbol tile pairs a picture with a word for pre-readers.

no_filler.evidence: Kid paragraphs cover observe and record, count to find the pattern, morning versus afternoon, and pattern versus one day with seasons. Adult paragraphs give the standards and key words, the scientific method and the reason afternoons are warmest, the named mistakes, and what the lab does. The filler gate passes and nothing repeats template text.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at iPhone 13 width (390 px) in light and dark and at 1200 px desktop for every step before and after Show me. Fixed from screenshots: day labels in the block chart were clipped at the column edge (icon and label moved left), the warm step's finished view was only a list (now a paired 9 am / 2 pm bar chart), and sort cards were made taller on phones so the longest card keeps a readable font. Symbol tiles are about 100 x 96 px, day slots 54 px tall, thermometers 150 px wide and the whole thermometer is the tap target.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button twin with a descriptive aria-label, wrong choices included ('Record Monday as sunny', 'Move Monday into the Sunny column', 'Monday: the 9 am thermometer was warmer', 'Put It snowed on my birthday in A pattern', 'Put Frost on the grass in Summer'). The canvas aria-label updates with each reply, weather symbols always carry a word as well as a picture, the challenge uses real buttons and a polite live region, and the browser gate's axe WCAG 2.1 AA run is clean in both themes on desktop and phone.

sources: NGSS (2013) K-ESS2-1 Earth's Systems: 'Use and share observations of local weather conditions to describe patterns over time', with its clarification statement (numbers of sunny, windy and rainy days in a month; relative temperature, e.g. cooler in the morning than in the afternoon)

DfE (2013) National Curriculum in England: science programmes of study, Year 1 Seasonal changes ('observe changes across the four seasons'; 'observe and describe weather associated with the seasons and how day length varies')
Met Office (Learn about weather / Met Office for schools): keeping a weather diary; why the warmest part of the day is usually mid-afternoon; UK seasons and climate averages
NOAA SciJinks / National Weather Service education pages on daily temperature change (the daily maximum usually comes in mid to late afternoon)
